title: A Framework for Evaluating and Benchmarking Concept Drift Detection Methods
authors: Cerqueira, V.; Gomes, H.M.; Heyden, M.; Pfahringer, B.; Bifet, A.
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
tldr: A unified benchmarking framework for concept drift detection in data streams introduces controlled drift simulation on real datasets, timing-aware evaluation metrics, and leave-one-dataset-out hyperparameter optimization.
problem_and_motivation: Concept drift detection methods lack unified evaluation practices, with studies relying on oversimplified synthetic data, incompatible metrics, and opaque hyperparameter selection, making fair comparisons unreliable.
approach: A drift simulation framework injects controlled distributional changes into 7 real-world datasets via Monte Carlo trials.
Four drift types simulated: class prior, class label swap, feature permutation, and feature filtering.
An acceptable detection window defines true positives, false negatives, and false positives for timing-aware evaluation.
New evaluation metrics include F1 detection score, normalized detection time (NDT), episode recall, alarm rate, and false alarm rate.
Leave-one-dataset-out cross-validation protocol optimizes detector hyperparameters on held-out datasets.
14 drift detection methods benchmarked using a Hoeffding Tree classifier within CapyMOA Python library.
findings: SEED and STEPD exhibit the most consistent performance across all drift types and abruptness conditions.
Gradual drifts are systematically harder to detect than abrupt ones, with most detectors showing lower median F1 scores.
Unsupervised detectors ABCD(X) and STUDD perform strongly on feature-space drifts but poorly on label-based changes.
PH and EWMA consistently rank among the worst performers across nearly all scenarios.
SEED achieves the best F1 rank while maintaining a moderate false alarm rate, making it the most balanced detector overall.
The relative ranking of detectors is largely preserved across five different classifiers, confirming results are not learner-specific.
Hyperparameter optimization improves median F1 for most detectors except SEED.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: Contributes a unified benchmarking framework for evaluating concept drift detection methods in data streams. Introduces drift simulation framework, timing-aware evaluation metrics, and leave-one-dataset-out hyperparameter optimization protocol.
directly_justifies: SEED, STEPD, and ABCD consistently outperform other detectors across distinct drift types and abruptness conditions.
Gradual drifts are systematically harder to detect than abrupt ones.
Hyperparameter optimization using leave-one-dataset-out yields improvements for most detectors.
Unsupervised detectors excel on feature-space drifts but fail on label-based distribution changes.
The relative ranking of detectors is largely preserved across five different classifiers.
limits: Limited to one classifier (Hoeffding Tree) in main experiments, though supplementary tests reported.
Only four drift types are simulated, excluding incremental drift, noise injection, etc.
Random shuffling removes inherent temporal structure from real-world data.
The prequential workflow assumes immediate label availability, which is unrealistic in many domains.

limitations: Limited to one classifier (Hoeffding Tree) in main experiments, though supplementary tests on four additional classifiers are reported.
Only four drift types are simulated, excluding incremental drift, noise injection, heteroskedasticity, and temporal dependencies.
Random shuffling removes inherent temporal structure from real-world data to isolate controlled drift injection.
Only 7 real-world datasets used, which may not represent the full diversity of stream dynamics.
The prequential workflow assumes immediate label availability, which is unrealistic in many real-world domains with verification delay.
